turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Michelle King, date of birth 01/05/1986, mrnq27631. New patient visit for acid reflux. Past medical history of anxiety and seasonal allergies. Hello, are you mrs. King?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I am.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: I'm dr. Phillips. Very nice to meet you.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: You as well.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: How can I help you today?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Well, my primary doctor, dr. Scott, he referred me here.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I've just got really bad acid reflux.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. Can you tell me more about it?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah. Though I mean I... Right now, I take 40 milligrams of omeprazole twice a day. Some days, it is fine, but others are just really bad.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: What do you feel?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: It feels like burning.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: In your chest?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yes, in my chest and also in my throat.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: In your throat and chest. All right. Any difficulty with swallowing? Feels like food or liquids kinda get stuck?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. That's good. Any abdominal pain?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: No, not really.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Nausea or vomiting, changes in bowel movements?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Constipation, diarrhea, rectal bleeding?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Nope.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. Very good. And how long have you had this problem?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I've had acid reflux since I was around 12, but it has gotten worse over the past few years.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. And how long have you been on the omeprazole?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: On the way, it is now I think about a year.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. Do you find that it's done anything for you in the past?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I mean, I can tell it's helped because some days, I'll be fine, and then some days, I eat something and it feels terrible.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Are there any things that make your symptoms worse that you can pinpoint, like food choices or stress?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Sure. Probably stress and food choices sometimes.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. What things bother you?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Spicy foods, um, so I try not to eat them too often, but sometimes even drinking a soda can cause it.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: We do know that caffeine and caffeinated beverages will do that, even sodas. Um, even just the carbonation can cause that. How about tomato-based products or citrus products?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah, sometimes, but I still eat them.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. It's reassuring that you aren't having any difficulty swallowing, though. How's your weight been? Pretty stable?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I'd say pretty stable, although I haven't had much of an appetite for the past two months. I have been under a lot of work stress.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: What do you do for work?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I'm a paralegal.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. And any family history of gi issues?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Um, my grandmother had esophageal cancer.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: On your mom or dad's side?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Mom's side. And my mom had some issues like acid reflux, and she was taking some medication that coats the lining of your stomach.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. Have you ever had an upper endoscopy?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I think maybe when I was younger.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: But not in the last 10 years?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: No.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Have you ever tried any medication other than omeprazole?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Um, at one point I was on omeprazole and ranititine -dine. It did help. But other than that, those are the only medications I have taken.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Okay. Have a seat here, and let me listen to your heart and lungs, and then we can talk about a plan for you.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Okay.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: So normal physical exam per my new patient template, except for well-healed abdominal surgical scars noted. What's the surgical scar here on your abdomen from?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: I always forget about that surgery. I had it when I was a baby. My mom said my intestines were twisted, so I had to have surgery when I was around one month old.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Hm, gotcha. Okay. So let's talk about what you have going on. From what you've told me, it sounds like you've had a several-year history of gerd, which is the medical term for acid reflux. And recently your symptoms have been poorly controlled with the omeprazole, 40 milligrams twice daily. You've been having heartburn despite taking this medication, correct?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yes.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: And you've identified trigger foods like spicy foods, carbonated bev- beverages, citrus, and tomato-based foods, but you haven't cut these foods out of your diet completely yet. So the first thing I'd try is changing your diet because these foods can exacerbate your gerd, even though you're taking the ppi.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Okay, yeah, I could definitely do a better job of avoiding those foods.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Great. So stress is another trigger that we need to address. High stress can cause worsening of your symptoms.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Yeah, stress and anxiety are definitely big problems for me.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: So working on that may help with your gerd. Additionally, we can consider trying a different ppi since the only one you've tried up to this point is omeprazole. If you're okay with this, we can switch your omeprazole to nexium.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: That's fine with me. I'm definitely open to trying whatever.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Perfect. I will send a prescription for nexium 40 milligrams twice daily to your pharmacy on file. I'll also recommend that you have a procedure called a egd, or upper endoscopy, to look for potential causes of the gerd. We'd sedate you and then pass a small camera through your mouth, down your throat, through your stomach, and end in the small intestines. We'd look for any ulcers or signs of precancerous or cancerous conditions that we can take biopsies at the same time if we see anything.

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: Okay. Can I schedule that today?

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Yeah. You can get scheduled at checkout desk. I'll have you follow up with me in the office for the egd so we can discuss the results and talk about how you're doing with the dietary, stress, and medication changes. How does all of that sound?

turns.label: Patient
turns.text: That sounds good.

turns.label: Clinician
turns.text: Perfect. I will walk you to the checkout desk. Be sure to call my office and let me know if anything changes or if you have problems before your egd and follow-up appointment. Please insert the procedure paragraph in the plan. I suspect that she likely has gerd with underlying functional etiology as well. Reassuringly, she has no unintentional weight loss and denies any dysphagia. If her egd is normal and her symptoms pers- persist despite a trial of nexium, we can consider a trial of protonix and obtain a ph-impedance study. This will allow us to rule out abnormal acid reflux exposure and to decipher between a functional etiology and hypersensitivity.
